answer: Viability and scalability are currently unproven; the concept is sensible but the plan rests on untested, and likely optimistic, assumptions. Revenue path: The model (per-jar fee to makers, mailer fee to customers, premium dashboard later) is plausible in structure, but no prices, unit economics, or financial model exist. The core claim, that a per-jar fee will undercut the cost of new jars, is the central economic bet and is untested and probably shaky. New glass jars typically cost roughly $1-3 in volume, while this model must cover a prepaid mailer, two-way postage on a heavy fragile glass item (easily $6-12+ round trip, plus outbound return shipping to the maker), wax removal, washing, sanitizing, inspection, breakage losses, labor, and software. On a pure cost basis, the fee needed to break even will almost certainly exceed new-jar cost, meaning the value proposition must rest on sustainability marketing premiums rather than savings. The assumption that costs fall with scale is only partly valid: postage, glass weight, and manual cleaning labor are largely variable and do not shrink much with volume. Key unvalidated assumptions: (1) Customer return behavior. The plan itself admits the biggest competitor is customer inaction, yet offers no data on return rates. Return rates for reuse programs are often low (commonly well under 30%), which cripples per-jar revenue and supply for refilling. (2) Maker willingness to pay and operate. Small makers must handle inbound jars, refilling, re-labeling, and quality control, and they have limited margins and time. Positive feedback from friends, family, and a few makers ('interesting') is not evidence of willingness to pay or repeat use. (3) Market size. No sizing was done; 'thousands of makers' times 'a small share' is not a model. Realistic volumes per small maker are low (tens to hundreds of candles a month), so jars per partner are limited and acquisition cost per partner matters greatly. (4) Jar heterogeneity. Each maker uses different jars, lids, and wax types, complicating cleaning standards, sorting, and logistics; logistics must also route each jar back to its originating maker, adding complexity and cost. Scalability: Operations are labor- and shipping-intensive, run from a shared kitchen with a manual process, and have no clear automation path. Scaling to thousands of jars requires a proper facility, food/safe-handling and wax-waste compliance considerations, and breakage/liability handling. The software dashboard scales well but is the least differentiating and least monetizable piece. The niche focus on small makers is also a scalability tension: small makers are fragmented and costly to acquire, with low volume each, while larger brands, who could provide volume, run in-house programs. Competition and defensibility are weak: no moat beyond focus, easy to replicate, and general reuse services (e.g., Loop-style models) or makers' own take-back or discount-incentive programs could absorb the need. Execution risk: Student team with a plausible skill mix (operations, product, data), but no legal entity, website, advisors, pricing, or financial model, and part-time commitment. Traction is minimal and anecdotal. Overall: an appealing, mission-driven concept with a sound problem observation, but currently an unvalidated hypothesis. The path to profit is not demonstrated. To raise viability, the team should: run a paid pilot to measure actual return rates and willingness to pay; build per-jar unit economics including shipping, breakage, and labor; consider alternatives like drop-off points at markets or local makers' shops, local-only hubs, or deposit/incentive mechanisms to improve return rates and cut postage; and size the market bottom-up. Prize funding for a controlled pilot is reasonable, but the current plan does not yet justify scaled investment.
